title: Profiling, algoritmos y rendimiento
scope: LESSONS_ONLY: title/tagline/job relevance, 8 outcomes, 33/33 theory/reference paragraphs, 9 theory code/output blocks, 9 callouts, 2 declared figures (1 currently renderable, 1 missing from registry), plus the section-specific interactive playground rendered inside Theory. I Do / We Do / You Do / self-check / exams excluded.

roadmap.T1: Medición: wall/CPU and memory profiling; benchmark fixture, warmup, variability.
roadmap.T2: Algoritmos: complexity/blocking; structures, vectorization, candidate reduction.
roadmap.T3: Memoria/I/O: dtypes, chunking, columnar; caching, invalidation, out-of-core.
roadmap.T4: Regresión: performance budget/tests; total cost, clarity, no microoptimization.
roadmap.gate: Reporte antes/después con el mismo resultado, dataset, hardware y límites; optimización reversible y justificada.

research_basis.use: perf_counter measures elapsed wall duration and includes sleep; process_time is process-wide user+system CPU and excludes sleep.
cProfile is recommended deterministic profiling; tottime excludes subcalls while cumtime includes them; internal vs cumulative answer different bottleneck questions.
autorange calibrates loop count until at least 0.2 s; repeat defaults to 5; benchmark setup is excluded and raw timing is affected by other programs.
benchmarking uses calibrated loops, warmups, multiple worker processes/values and records system/Python metadata; track-memory and tracemalloc measure different memory notions.
C extensions can explicitly register allocated blocks with PyTraceMalloc_Track and domains; C-extension allocation is not categorically invisible.
NumPy hooks CPU data allocations into tracemalloc and exposes np.lib.tracemalloc_domain, directly contradicting the blanket NumPy-exclusion statement.
array representations depend on C implementation/machine architecture; array('i') is C signed int and its actual itemsize is not guaranteed to be 4 bytes.

rejected_findings.claim: perf_counter/process_time definitions are reversed or unusable.
rejected_findings.evidence: Current Python docs support the source's basic wall-vs-process-CPU distinction.

rejected_findings.claim: dict/set average membership cannot be described as O(1) amortized.
rejected_findings.evidence: The source correctly qualifies it as amortized/average-style behavior rather than worst-case guarantee.

rejected_findings.claim: Enumerating every unordered ER pair is not O(n^2).
rejected_findings.evidence: n(n-1)/2 candidate enumeration is quadratic; the defect is in the blocking cost helper, not this asymptotic fact.

rejected_findings.claim: Using narrower fixed-width integer dtypes can never halve payload memory.
rejected_findings.evidence: int32 vs int64 does halve element payload when values fit; the defect is representing int32 with native array('i') and pretending the Python list has that bound.
Warmup is useful for steady-state benchmarks; the defect is the absolute 'first run lies' wording and failure to separate cold-start as a legitimate target.

rejected_findings.claim: cProfile is inappropriate for locating Python hot paths.
rejected_findings.evidence: Python recommends cProfile for most users; the defect is hard-coded hottest-function logic and failure to distinguish internal vs cumulative timing.

rejected_findings.claim: RSS is the wrong metric for container/process memory limits.
rejected_findings.evidence: RSS/process-level memory is a relevant system-level quantity; tracemalloc answers a different allocation-attribution question.

rejected_findings.claim: The dbt-bigquery legacy id itself should simply be renamed.
rejected_findings.evidence: The source explicitly documents it as a stable URL/progress key; the learner-facing defect is the stale playground mapping, not the stable identifier itself.

rejected_findings.claim: The S37-where-time-goes bars are arithmetically inconsistent.
rejected_findings.evidence: 8+64+21+7=100; the defect is that the apparently measured percentages have no benchmark provenance.

findings.summary: S37 benchmarks S36-era signals although S36 remains REPAIR_REQUIRED.
findings.evidence: Roadmap prerequisite S36; continuation explicitly says only repaired machine-valid S36 artifacts may be optimized.
findings.attack: A fast benchmark of an invalid detector/ranking can institutionalize upstream defects.
findings.defense: Referencing prior work is pedagogically appropriate if its contracts are green.
findings.fix: Require machine-valid inherited fixture/results and carry S36 regression suite before any performance comparison.

findings.summary: The central before/after report has no executable manifest binding dataset hash, code commit, benchmark stage, hardware/runtime/library versions, repetitions and policy state.
findings.evidence: Prose demands dataset/hardware but snippets store none of these as artifacts.
findings.attack: Numbers cannot be reproduced or compared if either code, data, stage boundary or environment drifted.
findings.defense: The prose correctly names dataset and hardware as required context.
findings.fix: Create versioned BenchmarkManifest and BeforeAfterResult with hashes/environment/stage boundaries.

findings.summary: same_result is a string/static promise rather than an executed equivalence gate.
findings.evidence: section_contract lists same_result; profile helper checks only s>=0 and s2>=0; T4-B never compares outputs.
findings.attack: Different nonnegative outputs pass CE01.
findings.defense: The prose repeatedly states equivalence as the core rule.
findings.fix: Run baseline/candidate on identical keyed fixture and assert an explicit domain comparator.

findings.summary: Legacy id dbt-bigquery renders a simulated dbt model/tests/lineage playground inside S37 Theory.
findings.evidence: SectionView mapping for dbt-bigquery is dbt_model_daily_metrics and dbt tests, while S37 roadmap/source are profiling/performance.
findings.attack: A learner receives a complete practice activity from a different topic.
findings.defense: The stable id itself should remain for progress compatibility.
findings.fix: Keep id stable; replace only the playground mapping with S37 profiling/equivalence content.

findings.summary: S37-percentiles is declared in theory but absent from both bespoke FIGURES and all FIGURE_DATA registries, so FigureFrame returns null.
findings.evidence: FigureFrame returns null for unknown IDs; bespoke registry lacks S37-percentiles; data registries contain S37-where-time-goes but no S37-percentiles.
findings.attack: The intended tail-latency visual silently disappears from learner-facing theory.
findings.defense: Alt/caption metadata exists in the section source.
findings.fix: Add a registered figure with validated data or remove the dead declaration.

findings.summary: The missing figure's caption says p95=5 s with mean=200 ms, numerically incoherent under the usual empirical p95 interpretation for nonnegative latency.
findings.evidence: At least roughly 5% at or above 5000 ms already contributes about 250 ms to the mean before all other observations.
findings.attack: If the missing figure is repaired as written, it teaches impossible/incoherent summary statistics.
findings.defense: The intended lesson that tail latency can matter despite a low average is correct.
findings.fix: Use a coherent sample/distribution and derive mean/median/p95 from it.

findings.summary: Theory categorically says C-extension buffers such as NumPy/pandas are outside tracemalloc.
findings.evidence: Current NumPy explicitly hooks PyDataMem allocations into tracemalloc and exposes np.lib.tracemalloc_domain; Python C API permits extensions to register other domains.
findings.attack: Learners are told a current profiling capability does not exist.
findings.defense: tracemalloc is not RSS and can miss allocations that extensions do not track; that distinction is valid.
findings.fix: Say tracemalloc measures tracked allocations, not RSS; extension visibility depends on allocator/tracing integration, with NumPy as a positive example.

findings.summary: Wall, CPU and memory are measured on three separate path executions while result equivalence between them is not checked.
findings.evidence: profile_wall_cpu_mem calls path(n) once for wall, once for CPU, once under tracemalloc; only first and third outputs enter a nonnegative predicate.
findings.attack: Stateful/nondeterministic work can produce different outputs and states while reporting result=True.
findings.defense: Separate runs can reduce interference among measurement tools for a pure deterministic function.
findings.fix: Declare purity or snapshot/reset state; compare keyed outputs across runs and bind each measurement to the same fixture/version.

findings.summary: hot_function claims to name the hottest function but hardcodes only expensive-vs-cheap and uses internal tottime without explaining cumulative time.
findings.evidence: Return expression can only produce 'expensive' or 'cheap'; Python docs distinguish tottime from cumtime.
findings.attack: Any third/nested dominant function cannot be returned; high-level bottleneck may appear in cumulative rather than internal time.
findings.defense: For the current toy of two leaf helpers, expensive is predictably hotter.
findings.fix: Use pstats/argmax over the intended metric and teach internal vs cumulative timing.

findings.summary: T1-B/callout says 'La primera corrida miente' and publishing cold start deceives, contradicting the opening's correct caveat that cold start may be the target.
findings.evidence: Opening says if startup latency matters the first run is exactly the measurement; later callout uses an absolute prohibition.
findings.attack: Learners may erase a legitimate user-facing startup SLO.
findings.defense: Discarding warmup is appropriate when measuring steady-state algorithm throughput.
findings.fix: Name benchmark mode: cold-start and steady-state are separate experiments; never discard a target metric.

findings.summary: bench.py times five single executions of a tiny sum loop without calibration or process isolation.
findings.evidence: Current timeit autorange targets >=0.2 s; pyperf calibrates loops, warmups and multiple workers/values.
findings.attack: Timer/jitter overhead can be material relative to a very short workload and a 5-sample median can move with noise.
findings.defense: Five runs plus a warmup is better than a single timing and is simple for learners.
findings.fix: Use timeit.autorange or pyperf-style calibrated loops and record raw values/environment.

findings.summary: The benchmark reports median_ms_ok>=0, spread_ms_ok>=0 and warmup=True rather than benchmark evidence.
findings.evidence: Nonnegative timing/range are nearly tautological and warmup is a literal.
findings.attack: A noisy, meaningless or unexpectedly slow run remains green.
findings.defense: Exact times cannot be hard-coded across machines.
findings.fix: Persist actual measurements, variability, loop count and result checksum; assert only semantic invariants/budgets appropriate to a controlled runner.

findings.summary: blocking_cost assumes every block has floor(n/B) rows and drops n%B rows from its pair count.
findings.evidence: CE02: n=10,B=3 returns 9 blocked pairs; balanced complete partition 4,3,3 has 12.
findings.attack: The primary cost metric understates work and silently loses remainder population.
findings.defense: The nominal n=100,B=10 fixture divides evenly.
findings.fix: Compute cost from actual block membership/sizes, not a divisibility-only approximation.

findings.summary: blocking_cost has no domain validation.
findings.evidence: CE03/CE04 crash; CE05 reports 100% reduction for 10 blocks over 3 rows.
findings.attack: Invalid configurations look optimal or fail with incidental arithmetic exceptions.
findings.defense: Nominal fixture uses n=100,B=10.
findings.fix: Validate n>=2 and 1<=blocks<=n or explicitly define singleton/empty semantics.

findings.summary: Theory says recall remains the matching gate but S37 computes only pair count/reduction and inherits unvalidated S30 debt.
findings.evidence: No labeled pair fixture or recall assertion appears in theory code.
findings.attack: A blocking change can remove all true pairs and still appear as a 100% cost win.
findings.defense: The prose explicitly warns against sacrificing recall.
findings.fix: Run baseline/blocking over the same labeled fixture and assert candidate recall plus downstream-equivalence contract.

findings.summary: inverted_index builds city→IDs internally but returns only city→count, destroying the IDs needed to generate candidate pairs.
findings.evidence: return {k: len(v)}; no candidate pair generation or scorer input exists.
findings.attack: The code cannot perform the mechanism its paragraphs describe.
findings.defense: It accurately demonstrates block cardinality for the tiny fixture.
findings.fix: Return immutable IDs per key and generate canonical candidate pairs, then verify candidate reduction/recall.

findings.summary: Roadmap/heading promise vectorization but theory gives only a sentence and no executable contrast or decision rule.
findings.evidence: T2-B code is only defaultdict indexing; no array/vectorized operation is shown.
findings.attack: A required subtopic becomes a widow term rather than an operational skill.
findings.defense: Vectorization was introduced in S14 and S37 correctly prioritizes reducing candidate count first.
findings.fix: Add a small post-block vectorized-vs-loop example only after candidate reduction, preserving identical results.

findings.summary: array.array('i') is labeled int32 and expected output itemsize_i32=4 although Python defines it as native C signed int with architecture-dependent representation.
findings.evidence: Python array docs state actual representation depends on C implementation/machine and 'i' minimum size is 2 bytes.
findings.attack: The lesson's portable memory claim and expected output can fail on a supported architecture.
findings.defense: Most current student platforms use 4-byte C int and array('q') is commonly 8.
findings.fix: Use an explicitly fixed-width stack dtype (e.g. NumPy int32/int64) or label the stdlib demo native-int/native-long-long and avoid hard-coded 4.

findings.summary: bound_bytes is computed as len(Python-list)*array('i').itemsize even though data remains a Python list and no compact array is created/measured.
findings.evidence: data=list(range(10)); bound_bytes=len(data)*i32; bound_ok only compares i32<i64.
findings.attack: The reported memory bound ignores list pointers, Python integers, allocator overhead and chunk copies.
findings.defense: The comment says it is a bound 'si usamos int32', so it is intended as hypothetical payload arithmetic.
findings.fix: Actually construct/measure the target representation or name it payload_bytes_if_native_int, separate from peak/RSS.

findings.summary: chunks accepts invalid size values.
findings.evidence: CE06 size=0 raises incidental ValueError; CE07 negative size silently produces no chunks.
findings.attack: An invalid tuning parameter can erase processing or crash outside an explicit contract.
findings.defense: Nominal size=3 behaves correctly including remainder chunk.
findings.fix: Require positive integer chunk_size and test empty/remainder cases.

findings.summary: The outcome promises minimal columnar reading but code merely prints ['id','amount']; it never reads/project columns from a dataset.
findings.evidence: No file/table/columnar reader appears in theory code.
findings.attack: Learner cannot observe memory/I/O impact or verify unused blobs were not loaded.
findings.defense: The section intentionally stays stdlib-oriented and frames formats as a later-stack application.
findings.fix: Use a small introduced columnar-capable fixture/stack or narrow the outcome to projection planning and explicitly defer real columnar I/O.

findings.summary: cache_put writes a value then returns key in store, and the example prints this as hit=True.
findings.evidence: CE08: store is empty before call yet function returns True after insertion.
findings.attack: A cache miss followed by a write is taught as a cache hit.
findings.defense: The function does verify the write is present afterward.
findings.fix: Implement cache_get returning hit/miss before recomputation; keep put/write-success as a separate operation.

findings.summary: Invalidation is a literal string and key=(feature_set, cutoff) is insufficient for data revisions/backfills, code/scaler/detector/policy versions and source snapshot.
findings.evidence: invalidate_policy returns 'version_or_cutoff'; no invalidation operation or stale-entry test exists.
findings.attack: Same cutoff can contain revised data; same feature-set name can be produced by changed code/reference state.
findings.defense: Version+cutoff is a useful first mental model.
findings.fix: Use content/versioned dependency key and test miss after each relevant upstream change/backfill.

findings.summary: Out-of-core is promised but executable evidence is only the string 'chunk_if_needed'.
findings.evidence: No threshold, iterator/spill path, bounded peak or disk-backed operation exists.
findings.attack: The learner sees policy text rather than an out-of-core mechanism or measurable bound.
findings.defense: Chunking in T3-A introduces one building block.
findings.fix: Implement bounded streaming/chunk processing with measured peak and explicit spill/temporary-file policy if taught.

findings.summary: T4-A talks about p95 latency, memory and candidate budgets but code compares one hand-entered measured_ms=12 to 50.
findings.evidence: No repetitions, percentile, memory, candidates, fixture hash or CI-failing assertion.
findings.attack: The supposed regression test can be green without measuring the program at all.
findings.defense: The scalar inequality correctly illustrates the final budget comparison once a metric exists.
findings.fix: Feed measured metrics from the benchmark artifact; assert all declared budgets in pytest on controlled CI tiers.

findings.summary: budget_pass accepts impossible/nonfinite measurements.
findings.evidence: CE09 -1 ms and CE10 -inf both pass a 50 ms budget.
findings.attack: Corrupt measurements are treated as excellent performance.
findings.defense: Real timers normally produce nonnegative finite values.
findings.fix: Validate finite nonnegative measured/budget values and unit/schema before comparison.

findings.summary: Tagline requires same hardware while CI-light budget discussion provides no runner fingerprint/pinning or variance strategy.
findings.evidence: No CPU model, affinity, Python version, runner class or baseline metadata is captured; pyperf explicitly records such metadata.
findings.attack: A shared-runner change can fail/pass a wall-clock PR budget independent of code.
findings.defense: Absolute budgets can be valid on controlled/pinned runners, and prose asks for a hardware note.
findings.fix: Pin/fingerprint performance runners or use environment-aware regression thresholds; persist metadata.

findings.summary: Final before/after numbers are literals, not outputs of baseline/candidate benchmarks, and no functional equivalence is checked.
findings.evidence: before={ms:100,pairs:1_000_000}; after={ms:20,pairs:50_000}; micro_only=False literal.
findings.attack: The capstone-like headline can be satisfied with invented numbers.
findings.defense: The arithmetic 5x/20x example is internally correct for those nominal inputs.
findings.fix: Construct report from two BenchmarkResult artifacts with same manifest and explicit equivalence assertion.

findings.summary: pair_factor uses // and calls it 'cuántas veces menos pares', corrupting noninteger ratios.
findings.evidence: CE13: 100/60 should be 1.6667 but function returns 1.
findings.attack: A generic reporting helper systematically understates ratios except exact divisibility cases.
findings.defense: The nominal 1,000,000/50,000 happens to divide exactly to 20.
findings.fix: Use true ratio before/after as float and separately report reduction=1-after/before.

findings.summary: speedup/pair_factor do not validate positive finite denominators/counts.
findings.evidence: CE11/CE14 divide by zero; CE12 accepts negative time.
findings.attack: Invalid benchmark artifacts become exceptions or meaningless ratios.
findings.defense: Nominal fixtures use positive values.
findings.fix: Validate before>0, after>0 for ratios; define special policy for zero work and finite timings.

findings.summary: Reversible/justified optimization is central to tagline/gate but no artifact identifies the candidate change, baseline commit/config, rollback action or justification.
findings.evidence: Theory outputs contain no commit/diff/config/version/rollback reference.
findings.attack: A benchmark cannot be tied to the exact optimization or reversed reproducibly.
findings.defense: Git/PR mechanics were taught earlier and need not be retaught in depth.
findings.fix: Benchmark report must reference baseline/candidate commits/configs and documented rollback/revert path.

findings.summary: Since S27 the roadmap requires systematic pytest, yet S37's theory gates are print-only scripts with no assertions/regression tests.
findings.evidence: All nine theory snippets print outputs; none is a collected test despite T4-A explicitly promising tests that fail PRs.
findings.attack: Broken equivalence/performance contracts do not make CI fail.
findings.defense: Printouts are useful for explanatory labs.
findings.fix: Keep explanatory prints if desired but add collected pytest regressions for correctness and controlled performance gates.

findings.summary: Dense prose introduces wall/CPU, warmup, cold start, IQR, blocking, recall, scorer, dtypes, OOM, cutoff, out-of-core, spill, p95, CI light and microbenchmark with uneven first-use explanation.
findings.evidence: Some are glossed but several remain compressed or only expanded much later.
findings.attack: Advanced content becomes vocabulary decoding rather than performance reasoning, particularly for a prerequisite-aware but self-contained learner.
findings.defense: S37 is advanced and many terms were introduced earlier; current redaction has already glossed several English terms.
findings.fix: Spanish-first first occurrence plus concise operational definition; keep API identifiers in code formatting.

findings.summary: Job relevance claims 'con n grande, el wall time se duplica' without defining what doubled or the algorithm/input scaling relation.
findings.evidence: Large n alone does not imply exactly 2x wall time; complexity and change in n determine scaling.
findings.attack: It teaches a quantitative causal claim with no model or denominator.
findings.defense: The intended message is that regressions matter more at scale.
findings.fix: Replace with a bounded statement that small per-unit regressions can compound with n and must be measured on representative sizes.

findings.summary: The renderable where-time-goes figure states the job spends 8/64/21/7 percent in stages and says where time 'really' goes, but no benchmark/run/dataset/hardware produces those percentages.
findings.evidence: FIGURE_DATA hardcodes values; T1-B benchmark only runs sum-of-squares and never parses JSON/features/output stages.
findings.attack: The section's main epistemic rule is violated by its own visual: invented profiling numbers look measured.
findings.defense: The percentages sum to 100 and clearly illustrate why optimizing the largest stage matters.
findings.fix: Label as a hypothetical profile or derive the bars from a reproducible synthetic staged benchmark and show its manifest.

findings.summary: 'El mismo resultado' is never operationally defined for ordered rows, floating reductions, candidate sets/rankings or S36 scores.
findings.evidence: No comparator/tolerance/order/tie policy appears in theory, despite vectorization/chunking/blocking being able to alter order or floating accumulation.
findings.attack: Byte equality may reject valid numeric equivalents while permissive checks can hide changed rankings/decisions.
findings.defense: The phrase 'resultado funcional idéntico' conveys the correct high-level intent.
findings.fix: Define per-artifact equivalence: keyed records, canonical order only where nonsemantic, numeric tolerances with rationale, exact ranking/tie/policy invariants where semantic.

USABLE: perf_counter measures elapsed wall time and process_time measures process CPU excluding sleep
profile before optimizing; compare before/after on the same intended workload
all-pairs candidate enumeration grows quadratically and candidate reduction can dominate micro-optimization
blocking cost gains must be evaluated alongside candidate recall
dict/set/inverted indexes can reduce repeated scans
narrower fixed-width dtypes can reduce payload memory when values fit
chunking trades loop overhead for bounded working set
cache invalidation is part of cache design
performance budgets are useful only when fed by reproducible measurements
total engineering cost and clarity matter alongside runtime
PARTIAL: blocking cost with arbitrary block sizes
MISCONCEPTION_RISK: large n automatically doubles wall time
s>=0 on two executions proves same result
same selected/nominal fixture means same benchmark without hash/environment
five tiny single-call timings are robust benchmark evidence
floor(n/B) block size represents all n rows when n%B != 0
city-to-count is an inverted index usable by the scorer
len(Python list)*array itemsize is the job's memory bound
the strings version_or_cutoff and chunk_if_needed implement invalidation/out-of-core
measured_ms=12 literal is a performance regression test
integer floor pair_factor is a generic ratio
hard-coded False flags prove microoptimization/privacy/test gates
hard-coded stage percentages are measured profiling evidence
